comparison: Both evaluate claims about SAM transmethylation pathway upregulation (C4, C30-C37) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes convergence of RNAseq, isotope tracing, and metabolomics data. Peer reviewers confirm the finding with Reviewer 1 noting 'convincing data' and Reviewer 3 stating authors 'successfully show that the pathway is activated.' Peer R1 also includes C38 and C94 about remethylation, which OpenEval addresses separately in R2.

OpenEval R2 evaluates C38 and C94 (lack of remethylation pathway) as SUPPORTED based on isotope tracing. Peer R1 includes these claims in their overall SUPPORTED evaluation of pathway activation. Both agree the data supports the conclusion that homocysteine enters transsulfuration rather than remethylation.

OpenEval evaluates Ahcy RNAi effects (C39-C44) as SUPPORTED, finding data internally consistent. Peer review rates this UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 raising critical concern about SAH accumulation confounding interpretation and requesting validation with other pathway enzymes. This represents a significant disagreement - OpenEval accepts the evidence while peer reviewers question specificity. Peer R2 also includes C46 (MTA data) which OpenEval addresses separately in R12.

Perfect claim overlap (C5, C55-C60, C97). Both evaluate adenosine as systemic signal as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes converging metabolomics and RNAi evidence while acknowledging ex vivo measurement limitations. Peer Reviewer 1 describes findings as 'convincing' regarding adenosine's role in regulating systemic metabolism and development. Strong agreement.

Perfect claim overlap (C61-C63, C100). Both evaluate Ahcy RNAi immune phenotypes as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate acknowledgment that phenotype results from both pathway suppression and adenosine loss. Peer Reviewer 2 confirms 'increased evidence that SAM transmethylation is directly required for encapsulation.' Strong agreement on the data quality and interpretation.

OpenEval R6 addresses adenosine recycling enzyme expression (C67-C69, C107) as SUPPORTED. Peer R5 covers broader claims including these plus isotope tracing data (C71-C76, C108), all rated SUPPORTED. Both affirm the upregulation of Adk3 and Ak1 upon infection. Peer reviewers emphasize the functional contribution of adenosine recycling to immune cell function.

OpenEval R7 evaluates isotope tracing showing adenosine recycling to SAM (C71-C76, C108) as SUPPORTED, noting physical coupling inference is speculative. Peer R5 includes these claims in broader SUPPORTED evaluation, with Reviewer 1 confirming 'recycling of adenosine to ATP, and ultimately SAM, contributes meaningfully.' Both accept the data while recognizing mechanistic inferences.

OpenEval R8 evaluates Adk3 RNAi phenotypes (C77-C82, C109-C112) as SUPPORTED. Peer R6 evaluates broader set including both Adk3 and Ak1 RNAi (C6-C7, C77-C87, C109-C115) as SUPPORTED. Both affirm that genetic experiments demonstrate adenosine recycling is required for immune response. Strong agreement on the functional requirement.

OpenEval R9 evaluates Ak1 RNAi phenotypes (C83-C87, C113-C115) as SUPPORTED, noting consistency with Adk3 results. Peer R6 includes these claims in comprehensive SUPPORTED evaluation of both enzymes' requirement. Both agree the data converge on adenosine recycling being necessary for immune function.

OpenEval R10 evaluates summary claims C6-C7 as SUPPORTED, noting they accurately summarize RNAi findings. Peer R6 includes these in broader SUPPORTED evaluation with extensive experimental claims. Both treat these as valid summary statements of the main findings.

Perfect claim overlap (C8-C9, C116-C119). OpenEval rates the adenosine release model as UNCERTAIN, noting it's a speculative hypothesis requiring validation. Peer review rates it SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 stating 'convincing data supports this idea' while acknowledging mechanistic details remain unknown. Disagreement on confidence level - OpenEval more cautious about untested hypothesis, peer reviewers more accepting of the model.

OpenEval R12 evaluates MTA data (C45-C46) as UNCERTAIN due to interpretation difficulties from SAH accumulation. Peer R2 includes C46 in UNCERTAIN evaluation of Ahcy RNAi, with concerns about confounding effects. Both express uncertainty about this aspect, though peer focus is on broader validation needs.

OpenEval R12 includes C45 (MTA data) rated UNCERTAIN. Peer R8 includes C45 in transsulfuration pathway claims rated SUPPORTED without explicit challenge. Peer reviewers accept the data presentation while OpenEval notes interpretation difficulties. Minor disagreement on confidence.

High claim overlap (C47-C52). OpenEval rates transsulfuration pathway data as UNCERTAIN, noting the alternative pathway is speculative and requires investigation. Peer review rates as SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 noting findings are 'robust and support most of the authors' claims.' Disagreement - OpenEval more cautious about speculative pathway, peer reviewers accept the data as presented.

Perfect claim overlap (C70). OpenEval rates metabolic redirection inference as UNCERTAIN, noting it's reasonable but requires experimental support. Peer review rates as SUPPORTED without challenge, accepting it as valid inference from gene expression. Disagreement on confidence level for this inference.

OpenEval R15 evaluates prior work citations (C1, C10-C15, C53-C54) as SUPPORTED. Peer R9 includes these in broader evaluation of all background/citation claims as SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 praising presentation quality. Both agree background context is accurate and well-presented.

OpenEval R16 evaluates biochemical background knowledge (C2-C3, C16-C28) as SUPPORTED. Peer R9 includes these in comprehensive SUPPORTED evaluation of all background claims. Both accept the biochemical context as accurate and appropriately cited.

OpenEval R17 evaluates literature citations (C29, C64-C66, C88-C106) as SUPPORTED. Peer R9 includes these in broad SUPPORTED evaluation of background and citations. Both agree the cited literature is accurately represented and provides appropriate context for conservation of SAM pathway function.
